# Web Game Engines: Pros, Cons & Longevity

## Web-Native Engines (built for the browser)

### **Phaser 3**
| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Pure JS/TS, zero install friction | 2D only (no native 3D) |
| Massive community, huge asset marketplace | Can get messy at scale; no built-in ECS |
| Runs in every browser, tiny load times | No official multi-platform target (web only) |
| Huge tutorial ecosystem, very beginner-friendly | Performance ceiling for heavy scenes |
| **Longevity: Very high.** ~10+ years old, backed by Phaser Foundation, steady releases. Extremely unlikely to die. | |

### **Babylon.js**
| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Full 3D, backed by **Microsoft** (funded, employed devs) | Steeper learning curve than Phaser |
| Built-in physics, audio, particles, GUI, GUI editor (Playground) | No official 2D pipeline (you bolt it on) |
| Excellent TypeScript support, great docs | Smaller ecosystem of ready-made assets vs. Unity/Unreal |
| Sandboxing, multiplayer networking built in | Less "game engine" feel out of the box; more "3D library you assemble" |
| **Longevity: Very high.** Microsoft's direct backing + active OSS. Likely 10+ more years. | |

### **Three.js**
| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| The de-facto standard for web 3D; runs *everywhere* | It's a **library**, not an engine. No game loop, physics, input, etc. |
| Enormous community, plugins, examples | You'll be wiring together 5+ libraries for a real game |
| Constant innovation (WebGPU, TSL, etc.) | No built-in scene graph editor, no build tooling |
| **Longevity: Extremely high.** It's the web's "OpenGL wrapper" equivalent. Will outlive most engines. | |

### **PlayCanvas**
| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Full 3D + 2D, **free cloud editor** (no local install) | Smaller community than the big names |
| Built-in ECS, physics, animation, GUI, multiplayer | Backed by a smaller company; risk if they pivot |
| Exports to web, mobile, desktop | Fewer third-party plugins/assets |
| **Longevity: Moderate-High.** Active and growing, but one-company dependency is a mild risk. | |

---

## Traditional Engines with Web Export

### **Unity (WebGL build)**
| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Most mature 2D/3D toolset, huge asset store | **WebGL builds are heavy** (1-5+ MB initial load, 30-60 MB+ for 3D) |
| C# / full IDE, massive tutorial base | **Unity's licensing drama (2023)** damaged trust; still recovering |
| Can target web *and* native from one codebase | WebGL is a **second-class** target; no native DOM, limited audio, no WebGPU yet |
| **Longevity: High but uncertain.** Ubiquitous, but the company's erratic decisions create real risk. | |

### **Godot 4 (HTML5/Web export)**
| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Free, fully open-source, no royalties, no corporate risk** | Web export is still **experimental / "best effort"**; not the primary target |
| Lightweight editor, fast iteration | WebGL2-only export; WebGPU support still in progress |
| 2D is first-class (excellent), 3D is solid | Web builds are slower than native; memory limits in browsers |
| Growing fast, strong community | Smaller asset ecosystem than Unity |
| **Longevity: Very high.** Community-governed (Godot Foundation), no single company can kill it. Best "insurance" pick. | |

### **Unreal Engine (Web build)**
| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
 | **Web support is extremely limited / effectively unsupported for real games.** You can do a tech demo, not a shipped game. |
| | Massive file sizes, no real browser game pipeline |
| | **Verdict: skip for web games.** It's a native engine that *can* technically compile to WASM. |

---

## Quick "Which Should I Pick?" Guide

| Your situation | Best fit |
|---|---|
| 2D web game, want to ship fast | **Phaser 3** |
| 3D web game, want a full engine | **Babylon.js** or **PlayCanvas** |
| 3D web game, want max control / WebGPU | **Three.js** (+ your own game loop) |
| Want one codebase → web + native, open-source | **Godot 4** |
| Already know C#, want the biggest asset store | **Unity WebGL** (accept the bloat) |
| Don't want to install anything, want a browser editor | **PlayCanvas** or **Construct 3** |

---

## Longevity "Bonus Points" Ranking

1. **Three.js** – foundational web library; will be around as long as the web itself.
2. **Godot** – community-governed, no corporate kill-switch.
3. **Phaser 3** – decade-old, foundation-backed, web-native.
4. **Babylon.js** – Microsoft-funded, but also a healthy OSS community.
5. **PlayCanvas** – solid but single-company risk.
6. **Unity** – dominant but corporate-fragile.
7. **Unreal (web)** – not really a web engine.

If "unlikely to be outdated soon" is your top criterion, **Godot** (for 2D/mixed) and **Babylon.js / Three.js** (for 3D) are the safest bets right now.
